rv.q: Carrie Cracknell's sweeping and epic production of stylishly sculpted ensemble work...makes us uncomfortably, insistently aware of the modern-day parallels.
Cracknell’s stealthily exacting production exerts an iron grip.

From the arresting opening, in which people bent almost double battle their way through a dust storm, to the haunting final vignette, this is a high-class, highly memorable - sometimes indelible - production.
At almost three hours, the production is overly long and you feel every second.
But somehow this production still doesn’t have the aesthetic or thematic boldness to link together its two halves.

For this mercy we must be grateful — although it is still repetitive, thanks to recurring myths about California, the legend of the jailbird son’s conviction and the sometimes comically hokey chit-chat.

In the end it’s absolutely fine, but the NT has a history of bringing overwhelming resources to bear on its revivals of classics to create something truly once in a lifetime; this feels underpowered by those standards.
Still, it is hard to feel the need for this theatrical version.
There is no lack of things to admire in this The Grapes of Wrath, but numbingly little to enjoy.
A harrowing evening and a memorable one.
Though this production doesn't scale epic heights, it is still extremely moving, not least in its almost biblical final moments.
Cracknell's production has an enthralling, wordless opening section
This stage version of The Grapes of Wrath often becomes a trial of the endurance of the audience’s spirit as it impresses and depresses in more or less equal measures.
By any means this is not an easy-breezy show to experience, but it sinks into your soul in a way that only an epic does.

cn.t: Cracknell's epic production of Steinbeck's Depression-era classic earns praise for striking staging and strong performances, particularly Cherry Jones, but critics split on whether Galati's reverent 1988 adaptation feels vital or overly bleak and sluggish.
